title: Natural Coastal Protection and Urban Settlement Patterns: A Multi‐Region Analysis of Wave Sheltering Effects on Coastal Urbanization
content:
Abstract

Coastal urbanization is accelerating globally, yet the role of natural coastal protection in shaping settlement patterns remains poorly understood. We examine how wave climate influences coastal population distribution by integrating global wave analysis data from the Copernicus Marine Service (CMEMS, January 2023–May 2025) with high-resolution population metrics (WorldPop) across five geomorphologically diverse coastal regions (Tokyo Bay, Melbourne, New York, Pearl River Delta, Yangtze River Delta). A dual-model spatial framework—combining a coastal distance-decay model and a regional neighborhood-average model—quantifies inland wave influence. Beyond the conventional mean significant wave height, we derive the deep-water wave energy flux P $P$ and decompose the wave field into its swell and wind-sea partitions. In Japan, the swell-only metrics match or exceed the explanatory power of total-wave metrics while the wind-sea component is generally weaker, consistent with a contribution from swell filtering; the relative performance of wave metrics varies among regions. To assess whether this signal could reflect the geometry of flat alluvial terrain, we further compute terrain slope from 30 m SRTM data and report partial correlations controlling for slope; the wave–population relationship persists with only marginal attenuation, indicating that wave climate carries explanatory power beyond terrain geometry alone. The proposed framework offers a physically grounded, quantitative tool for assessing natural coastal resilience and has implications for sustainable urban planning under climate change.
